\section[o ladrão]{o ladrão — the thief}

\label{lesson:PT-C386-ladrao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for legal, then the Portuguese for illegal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o ladrão}
\textbf{o ladrão} — \textquotedblleft{}the thief\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O ladrão fugiu pela janela.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The thief escaped through the window.}
\end{quote}

Plural \emph{os ladrões}; feminine \emph{a ladra}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ladrão} is inherited from Latin \emph{latrō, latrōnis} \textquotedblleft{}a hired servant, a mercenary\textquotedblright{}, later \textquotedblleft{}a robber\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o ladrão}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o ladrão}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o ladrão}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for legal, then the Portuguese for illegal, then say \emph{o ladrão} again
\end{itemize}

\section[acusar]{acusar — to accuse}

\label{lesson:PT-C386-acusar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for illegal, then the Portuguese for the thief.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acusar}
\textbf{acusar} — \textquotedblleft{}to accuse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Acusaram o vizinho de roubar a bicicleta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They accused the neighbour of stealing the bicycle.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Acusar alguém de} + noun or infinitive.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acusar} is inherited from Latin \emph{accūsāre} \textquotedblleft{}to call to account, to accuse\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{ad} and \emph{causa} \textquotedblleft{}cause, lawsuit\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{acusar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{acusar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for illegal, then the Portuguese for the thief, then say \emph{acusar} again
\end{itemize}

\section[a acusação]{a acusação — the accusation, the charge; the prosecution}

\label{lesson:PT-C386-acusacao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the thief, then the Portuguese for to accuse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a acusação}
\textbf{a acusação} — \textquotedblleft{}the accusation, the charge; the prosecution\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele negou a acusação.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He denied the accusation.}
\end{quote}

In court, \emph{a acusação} is also the prosecution.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acusação} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{accūsātiō} \textquotedblleft{}accusation, indictment\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{accūsāre}, on \emph{causa} \textquotedblleft{}lawsuit\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a acusação}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a acusação}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a acusação}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the thief, then the Portuguese for to accuse, then say \emph{a acusação} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a acusação mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The accusation, the charge; the prosecution\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[lícito]{lícito — lawful, permissible}

\label{lesson:PT-C386-licito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to accuse, then the Portuguese for the accusation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lícito}
\textbf{lícito} — \textquotedblleft{}lawful, permissible\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Não é lícito usar fotografias de outras pessoas sem autorização.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is not lawful to use other people's photographs without permission.}
\end{quote}

Formal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lícito} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{licitus} \textquotedblleft{}lawful, allowed\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{licēre} \textquotedblleft{}to be allowed\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to accuse, then the Portuguese for the accusation, then say \emph{lícito} again

\section[ilícito]{ilícito — unlawful, illicit}

\label{lesson:PT-C386-ilicito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the accusation, then the Portuguese for lawful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ilícito}
\textbf{ilícito} — \textquotedblleft{}unlawful, illicit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A polícia descobriu um negócio ilícito.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police uncovered an illicit business.}
\end{quote}

The opposite of \emph{lícito}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ilícito} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{illicitus} \textquotedblleft{}not allowed, unlawful\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{licitus} \textquotedblleft{}allowed\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{licēre} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ilícito}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the accusation, then the Portuguese for lawful, then say \emph{ilícito} again
